title: People-Powered Education: How Slice Teams Could Transform the Department for Education
author: Dr. James Mannion
summary: Drawing on twelve years spent helping schools implement change, Mannion introduces the "slice team", a small, diverse group drawn from every layer of a system and brought together to solve a shared problem, as the central engine of durable reform. He then extends the idea from schools to government, publishing an independent green paper that reimagines the Department for Education as a set of interlocking horizontal, vertical, and lateral slice teams. This is pitched as a new kind of devolution: rather than handing power to whoever controls a place, slice politics distributes it to the people with the most knowledge, experience, and stake in an issue, while preserving national democratic accountability.
points: A slice team is a small, diverse group drawn from every layer of a system, whoever has a valid perspective on the problem gets a seat at the table.
Slice teams improve change in two ways: better decisions (blind spots exposed, solutions stress-tested) and unprecedented buy-in (staff feel seen, heard and respected).

The green paper applies the model to the Department for Education through three structures, horizontal (senior policy leads), vertical (ground-up lived/professional experience) and lateral (geographic connection) slice teams.
Slice politics is framed as a different kind of devolution: power distributed by knowledge, experience and stake rather than by geography, while keeping national accountability intact.
Research across health and education is cited that change driven by representative teams is around five times more likely to take hold and endure than top-down reform.
quotes: A slice team is a small, diverse group of people drawn from every layer of a system and brought together to solve a shared problem.
When staff can see that they’re genuinely represented, they feel seen, heard and respected. Change stops being something done to them and becomes something they’re helping to shape
Rather than simply handing power to whoever happens to control a particular place, slice politics devolves power to the people with the most knowledge, experience and stake in an issue
It reimagines the policy environment by replacing top-down decision-making with representative, participatory, evidence-informed teams known as slice teams.
Across sectors such as health and education, research shows that change driven by representative teams is around five times more likely to take hold and endure than reform imposed from the top.
The result is “initiative-itis” among the teaching profession and a growing sense that policy is done to schools rather than with them.
